analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to let workers earn up to two weeks of paid vacation a year.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Labor Committee in March 2024 and received no further action before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require nearly all employers to give workers one hour of paid leave for every 25 hours worked, up to 80 hours a year. Workers could use it for any reason, would not have to say why, and could not be required to find their own replacement. Unused leave would be paid out when a worker leaves a job, and employers could not punish workers for taking the leave.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 1.1 million people who work for pay in the US who receive little or no paid vacation, particularly low-wage and hourly workers: a full-time worker would earn about two weeks of paid leave a year, usable for any reason, paid at their usual rate. Tipped workers would be paid the full minimum wage while on leave rather than their reduced cash wage.

how_it_helps.text: Employers must provide at least 1 hour of paid annual leave for every 25 hours worked, capped at 80 hours in any 12-month period, with earning beginning on the first day of employment.
Leave may be used for any reason; the employer may not require the employee to disclose why, and may not require the employee to find a replacement worker.
Upon termination, an employee must be financially reimbursed for all unused earned leave, and workers rehired within 12 months get their accrued leave reinstated.
Tipped employees on leave must be paid the greater of the federal, state, or local minimum wage, rather than the tipped cash wage.

The bill makes it unlawful to retaliate against or discriminate against a worker for taking leave or filing a complaint, and gives workers a private right of action with attorney's fees and liquidated damages.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, who would bear the cost of paid time off — roughly two weeks of pay per full-time employee per year for those who currently offer no paid vacation, plus recordkeeping and scheduling adjustments. There is no small-business exemption; covered employers include any business that employs someone for 20 or more workweeks a year.

drawbacks.text: The mandate raises labor costs by up to 80 hours of pay per employee per year, and the bill sets no phase-in or small-business carve-out, which would fall hardest on small businesses and low-margin industries that employ many hourly workers.

The benefit is modest by international standards: 80 hours a year is the ceiling, only 40 hours of it can carry over to the next year, and workers cannot use any of it until the 60th calendar day of employment unless the employer voluntarily loans it.
Employers may reject scheduling requests for a bona fide business reason and may impose up to 14 days' notice, so in practice managers retain substantial control over when leave is actually taken.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to workers is real but bounded — about two weeks of paid leave a year at most, less for part-timers, with no use in the first two months. The cost to employers is significant in aggregate but modest per worker, and the no-replacement-required and no-questions-asked provisions would meaningfully change leave-taking for the workers least likely to have any today. An honest supporter would acknowledge the small-business cost question and that employers keep scheduling discretion.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, which took no action, so it died there when the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Bernard Sanders (I-VT), joined by Alex Padilla (D-CA) and three other Democratic cosponsors, introduced the bill on March 20, 2024.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action followed, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2025 with the bill still in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers, especially those with low paid-leave usage today, are better off because the bill never advanced; workers without paid vacation gained nothing. The outcome is what routinely happens to labor bills introduced by a small bloc in the minority without a path to a floor vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who would have paid for the leave

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no other senators signed on over the rest of the session.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor was an Independent who caucuses with Democrats and all four cosponsors were Democrats or independents; no Republican supported it and no vote was ever held.

industries.industry: Employers without paid vacation (retail, food service, hospitality, small businesses)
industries.note: They would owe up to 80 hours of paid leave per employee per year with no small-business exemption, a direct payroll cost. The industries that most often lack paid vacation would bear the largest cost relative to revenue.

industries.industry: Larger firms that already offer paid vacation
industries.note: For employers that already provide two or more weeks of paid leave, the mandate is mostly moot, and the bill explicitly preserves any more generous benefit already offered. Their remaining costs are recordkeeping and payout of accrued leave on termination.
